newsitem.title: italy: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI SAVOURS FIRST HOME WIN.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI SAVOURS FIRST HOME WIN.

text.p: Olympic and world giant slalom champion Deborah Compagnoni found out at last on Sunday what it was like to win in Italy.

The greatest woman Alpine skier that Italy has produced -- she was her country's first to win gold medals at successive Olympics in 1992 and 1994 -- won a giant in Cortina d'Ampezzo for her third consecutive victory.
It was the first World Cup win on home snow since she started out on the circuit in 1987.
Compagnoni, who has now won four World Cup races this season, clocked a combined time of two minutes 38.25 seconds through falling snow on the Olimpia delle Tofane piste.
Germany's Katja Seizinger was second in 2:38.84 and Switzerland's Sonja Nef third in 2:39.67.
"I have won in Italy at last, I've cracked it," the 26-year-old Compagnoni, who dominates the giant slalom standings with 460 points after six races, told reporters.
The other two were also delighted, with Nef the happiest after securing her first podium exactly a year to the day since the last -- a slalom win in Sestriere.
"I'm really getting my rhythm back. Now I can really go for it again," the Swiss skier said.
Seizinger, who is skiing well in all disciplines, said she had not really expected to do so well on Sunday.
"Right now I don't really know which I am strongest in," she said. "My giant is maybe better than my downhill.
Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg finished fourth to stay comfortably ahead in the overall World Cup standings.
There was heartbreak for Slovenia's leading hope Urska Hrovat however, who tore the cruciate ligaments in her right knee in a fall just metres from the finish line.
Hrovat lay slumped in the finish area and sobbed despairingly as she received treatment. Officials confirmed that she would be out for the rest of the season.

The giant slalom triumph was the eighth of the season for the Italian women, who have won the last five races including Friday's downhill which Isolde Kostner shared with Heidi Zurbriggen of Switzerland after a dead heat.
Their success, coupled with a return to form by Alberto Tomba, is sure to increase to fever pitch the pressure on them going in to the world championships next week.
The championships open in Sestriere on February 2.
Compagnoni said she would be going home to Santa Caterina Valfurva later on Sunday for some light training.
"I will do a few evening slaloms to get used to the timetable more than the lights," she said.
"In Sestriere it is so well lit that it almost better than sunlight.. But the time could cause problems."
The second legs of the slaloms at the world championships will be run at night under floodlights.
Compagnoni made some mistakes in the first leg but corrected them by turning on the power lower down the slope.
"It was less tiring in the second," she said. "I had to do a lot more on the first -- I attacked for most of it."
Italy's Isolde Kostner, who won Friday's downhill and Saturday's super-G, missed a gate on the first leg.
Compatriot Sabina Panzanini, who won giants in Park City and Maribor, did not start due to a left Achilles tendon problem.

Team officials said Panzanini had returned home to nearby Merano and had decided to rest. They said the injury, which Panzanini first noticed in Maribor and which flared up in Zwiesel, did not threaten her world championships.

Compagnoni dedicated her win to Panzanini, with whom she spoke on Saturday night. "She's going to have 10 days of rest and will then do some light training. She came second in Bormio after a long pause so I think she will still do well," she said.
